pages.text:
*Days without rain: 120. Buckets from the spring: 6.*

Dusk settled over the shrine yard, turning the stone steps violet and grey. The village did not wait for the dark.

Teacher Luo, her red scarf tied tight against the chill, hoisted the heavy wooden drum onto a low stool. She tapped the skin with a mallet. *Thoom.* It was deep and round, vibrating right through the soles of everyone’s shoes.

Auntie Fen emerged from the shop with a basket of mismatched pots. “One for the left side,” she instructed, handing a brass ladle to a farmer. “Two for the right. Do not let them touch.”

The children formed a semicircle. Hua stood on a wooden bench, her yellow ribbon bright against the twilight. She pointed to groups with the calm authority of a class monitor who had finally found a room large enough for her energy. “Group one, clap on the beat. Group two, shake the spoons on the off-beat.”

Tao stood in the center, holding a thick drumstick. He looked at the stick. Then at the drum. Then at his boots. His face was solemn, as if he were about to sign a treaty rather than make noise.

He raised the stick.

*Crack.*

The sound was sharp and sudden. It sent a startle through the nearby sparrows, who scattered into the violet air like a handful of thrown seeds.
pages.image: Dusk in a stone shrine yard, Hua in a red jacket and yellow ribbon standing on a wooden bench organizing villagers, Tao in yellow rain boots holding a drumstick, Auntie Fen in a purple apron handing out pots, a large wooden drum on a stool, warm lantern light.

pages.text:
The stars appeared one by one, first faint, then bright, until the sky was a scattering of cold fire. The air was still, holding its breath.

Yeye Gu leaned on his cane, his long white eyebrows rising in the moonlight. “Today is the second day of the second month,” he said, his voice thin but clear. “The day the dragon raises his head. We do not ask. We wait.”

Nainai took the bamboo stick out of her jacket. She did not cut a notch. Instead, she touched the last one she had made that morning, her fingers lingering on the rough edge. “Water finds a way,” she murmured, more to herself than the crowd. “Sometimes it needs help finding the way.”

Everyone turned their faces upward, toward the dark tree line where the bamboo stood silent and rigid.

Mei stepped to the edge of the yard. Her throat felt tight, a knot of dry cotton. She looked at the dark shapes of the trees, then at the empty space above them. She whispered, her voice barely a breath in the cool night air.

“Yun? Everyone is ready.”
pages.image: Night scene with stars, Yeye Gu in a brown vest leaning on a cane, Nainai touching a bamboo stick by a door, Mei in a blue jacket and straw hat standing at the edge of a yard looking up, tall dark bamboo trees against the starry sky.

pages.text:
A rustle moved through the tall stalks, a sound like dry paper turning. Then, slowly, a long green coil rose out of the bamboo grove. It was slender and graceful, pale gold scales catching the light from the lanterns strung along the shrine. Mist curled around his neck like a soft scarf.

The villagers gasped, a collective intake of breath that seemed to suck the air out of the yard. Then they went very still. No one screamed. No one ran. The quiet was so complete it felt like someone had put a lid on the world. The scent of wet earth and pine hung in the air, sharp and clean.

Yeye Gu took off his old cloth cap and held it to his chest. He bowed his head, not in fear, but in recognition.

A small child, standing near the front, tilted her head and said, out loud and clear, “He is so pretty.”

Yun stopped. His large amber eyes blinked, wide and wet. He looked down at the hundred faces below, and his body froze, trembling slightly in the cool night air.
pages.image: A long sea-green dragon with pale gold scales and soft branching antlers rising from dark bamboo, mist around his neck, villagers standing still in a lantern-lit yard, an old man in a brown vest holding his hat, a small child pointing, calm and respectful mood.

pages.text:
Yun rose higher, his long body curving above the shrine until he hung like a green question mark over the tile roofs. He reached into a small, dark cloud gathered overhead, and the pearl under his chin began to glow with a soft, pulsing light that grew brighter with every second.

Mei watched the tension pull tight in his neck, her eyes tracking the way his whiskers twitched. His whole body trembled, a fine vibration running from his head to the tip of his tail, just like when Tao tried to hold in a sneeze during story time. He was holding it in. The rain. The thunder. The storm. All of it trapped inside him, heavy as a bucket of water he was afraid to spill.

In the stillness, a man near the back raised his hands halfway toward his ears. It was a small, unconscious gesture, but in the quiet yard, it felt like a door closing.

Mei pressed her thumb hard into the middle of her palm. The sharp pain cut through the fear, grounding her in her own skin. She looked at the man, then back at the dragon, whose eyes were closed tight against the coming sound.
pages.image: Dragon rising into a dark cloud, pearl under his chin glowing white, his body trembling, a man in the background raising hands toward his ears, Mei in the foreground pressing her thumb into her palm, lantern light reflecting on his scales.

pages.text:
Mei stepped into the empty space before the shrine, the cool earth pressing against the soles of her cloth shoes as a hundred pairs of eyes settled on her, heavy and warm, while the air in her chest felt packed tight like a box of books. She breathed in for four counts, held it, and let it go slowly.

Her mouth opened, and the words were there, waiting, small and fragile, but she pushed them out, not as a whisper, but as a real sound.

“Yun!”

The village went silent, drumsticks paused mid-air, and spoons stopped their shaking.

The dragon opened his eyes, wide and amber, holding a hope so fragile it looked ready to break, and he watched her, waiting.

Mei took another breath, her voice steady, even though her hands were shaking.

“We are here.”
pages.image: Mei standing alone in a stone yard, looking up at a dragon in the clouds, the dragon looking down at her with wide amber eyes, villagers frozen in the background with drums and pots, lanterns glowing, a moment of intense connection and courage.
